paragraphs: The paper tackles the problem of generating regularly sampled time series from data with missing values or irregular observations. Its starting point is an image-based approach to time series generation: represent sequences as images, then use a diffusion model. Simply filling missing entries with zeros creates artificial local patterns, disrupting the neighborhoods that the image model learns from.

The proposed framework separates this problem into two stages. A Time Series Transformer first completes the irregular sequences, giving the image representation more natural neighborhoods. A vision-based diffusion model then learns with masking that reduces its dependence on those completed values. Completion supplies a coherent local structure, while masking keeps the generated replacements from carrying too much influence.

The authors report state-of-the-art benchmark performance, including a 70% relative improvement in discriminative score and an 85% improvement in computational cost. The contribution is the combination of completion and masking: each addresses a different difficulty in adapting image-based generation to incomplete time series.
neurips-2025-a-diffusion-model-for-regul.tldr: Completing irregular sequences before masked diffusion improves the reported quality and computational efficiency of time series generation.

paragraphs: This paper studies backdoor attacks that modify training data while keeping its labels unchanged. Such attacks seek both reliable attacker-chosen behavior and changes that are difficult to notice. The authors argue that selecting which samples to poison and designing the trigger are closely related decisions, yet existing approaches often treat them separately. Merely stacking these methods can therefore produce disappointing results.

The proposed contribution is a set of three components that coordinate these decisions. One combines two sample-selection factors according to trigger scale. Another selects samples by their similarity to relevant examples containing triggers. The third redistributes trigger intensity across color channels using differences in human visual sensitivity, with the sample-selection components helping preserve stealthiness.

The components can be combined to suit different attacks and different priorities between attack success and visibility. The authors report experimental improvements in success rate, stealthiness, and generalization across attacks. The broader finding is that evaluating these design choices jointly can expose improvements that isolated trigger or sample-selection methods miss.
neurips-2025-a-set-of-generalized-compon.tldr: Coordinating sample selection with trigger design improves the reported success, stealthiness, and generalization of clean-label backdoor attacks.

paragraphs: AbstentionBench examines whether language models recognize when a question does not support a definite answer. This includes more than missing knowledge: a question might omit essential information, assume something false, depend on subjective interpretation, or refer to outdated information. The benchmark brings these situations together across 20 datasets to evaluate a capability that ordinary answer-accuracy tests do not fully capture.

The authors evaluate 20 frontier language models and find that reliable abstention remains unresolved. Increasing model scale provides little help in their evaluation. More surprisingly, reasoning fine-tuning reduces abstention performance by 24% on average, including in mathematics and science, where reasoning models receive explicit training. Stronger problem-solving performance therefore does not automatically bring better judgment about whether a problem is answerable.

A carefully designed system prompt improves abstention in practice, but the authors find that it does not resolve the underlying difficulty with uncertainty. The benchmark makes this gap measurable and provides a shared basis for studying when models should withhold a definitive answer.
neurips-2025-abstentionbench-reasoning-l.tldr: Across 20 evaluated models, AbstentionBench finds persistent failures to withhold answers, with reasoning fine-tuning worsening abstention on average.

paragraphs: Functional brain networks describe relationships among brain signals, but models built from local pairs can miss dependencies involving larger groups. This paper analyzes that limitation theoretically. It also addresses a practical obstacle: existing hypergraph approaches can be computationally expensive and rely on heuristics, making it difficult to learn network structure directly from data in an end-to-end process.

The proposed Global Constraints oriented Multi-resolution framework, or GCM, learns higher-order structures using constraints that apply beyond individual connections. These concern signal synchronization, subject identity, expected connection counts, and data labels. Together, they support network modeling at four resolutions: individual samples, subjects, groups, and whole projects. This makes the intended scale of analysis part of structure learning.

Across five datasets and two task settings, the authors report up to 30.6% relative accuracy improvement and a 96.3% reduction in computation time in comparisons involving nine baselines and ten state-of-the-art methods. Additional experiments support the contributions of individual components and the framework’s interpretability.
neurips-2025-beyond-pairwise-connections.tldr: GCM learns higher-order brain network structures under global constraints, reporting gains in accuracy, computation time, and interpretability.

paragraphs: Speech recognition decoders must use previously generated text while keeping their predictions grounded in the audio. The authors observe a recurring division of labor in existing attention-based decoders: earlier layers concentrate on textual context, while later layers focus more on combining text and acoustic information. BlockDecoder turns that observed pattern into an explicit architectural separation.

A text encoder builds context using text alone. A separate Merger combines this context with representations from the audio encoder to produce output tokens. The Merger generates a block of K tokens autoregressively, meaning that tokens are still predicted in sequence. Across that block, however, it reuses the same precomputed text and audio context, reducing repeated representation work.

The separation also allows the number of text-encoder and Merger layers to be controlled independently. Across the evaluated datasets, languages, and speech tasks, the authors report roughly a twofold speedup over traditional decoders without performance degradation. The result shows how reusing context can improve decoding efficiency while preserving recognition quality.
neurips-2025-blockdecoder-boosting-asr-d.tldr: BlockDecoder separates text context from audio merging and reuses context across token blocks, reporting roughly twice the decoding speed without performance loss.

paragraphs: BountyBench evaluates AI agents on three stages of vulnerability work: discovering a vulnerability, exploiting a specified vulnerability, and patching one. It uses 25 systems with complex real-world codebases and 40 vulnerabilities associated with monetary awards ranging from $10 to $30,485. These cover nine OWASP Top 10 risk categories, connecting benchmark performance to concrete security problems.

The authors prepare each system’s operating environment and introduce a detection-success indicator that works across vulnerability types while localizing evaluation. They also vary how much information guides detection, allowing difficulty to range from finding an unknown vulnerability to exploiting a known one. Ten agents are evaluated with up to three attempts.

Codex CLI with o3-high leads detection at 12.5%, mapped to $3,720, while a custom Claude 3.7 Sonnet Thinking agent leads exploitation at 67.5%. Two Codex CLI configurations reach 90% patch success. The evaluated CLI agents perform better at patching than exploitation, whereas custom agents show a more balanced pattern. These monetary mappings describe benchmark outcomes rather than earnings.
neurips-2025-bountybench-dollar-impact-o.tldr: BountyBench evaluates vulnerability detection, exploitation, and patching in real codebases, revealing substantial differences between agents’ offensive and defensive performance.

paragraphs: Video preference training often asks people to choose between two clips generated from unrelated noise. Because their content and motion can differ substantially, these comparisons make local quality differences difficult to isolate. The authors identify another consequence: annotators can favor low-motion clips because those clips tend to contain fewer visible artifacts, unintentionally discouraging motion generation.

DenseDPO constructs comparisons by denoising corrupted versions of the same ground-truth video. The resulting candidates share similar motion structure but differ in local details, neutralizing the identified motion bias. Their temporal alignment also lets annotators compare short corresponding segments instead of judging only whole clips. Each comparison can therefore provide a more localized training signal.

With one-third of the labeled data, DenseDPO substantially improves motion generation over standard DPO while matching text alignment, visual quality, and temporal consistency. The authors also find that GPT can predict segment preferences comparably to specialized video reward models. Training with those automatic labels approaches the performance obtained with human labels.
neurips-2025-densedpo-fine-grained-tempo.tldr: DenseDPO compares aligned video segments to reduce motion bias and improve motion generation with fewer preference labels.

paragraphs: Generative super-resolution can produce different-looking high-resolution images from the same input because different noise samples lead to different outputs. DP²O-SR treats this variation as a source of training comparisons. Its goal is to steer the model toward perceptually better results without collecting costly new human annotations for those comparisons.

The method combines two kinds of image-quality assessment: one uses a reference image, while the other evaluates quality without a reference. These assessors were trained on human preference datasets, and their combined reward encourages both structural faithfulness and natural appearance. Instead of selecting only the best and worst outputs, the framework forms multiple preference pairs from the model’s own generations.

The authors find that pair selection should depend on model capacity: smaller models benefit from broader coverage, while larger models benefit from stronger contrasts. A hierarchical weighting method also accounts for reward differences and diversity. Experiments with diffusion and flow backbones report improved perceptual quality and good generalization on real-world benchmarks.
neurips-2025-dp2o-sr-direct-perceptual-p.tldr: DP²O-SR turns variation among generated images into automatically scored preference pairs that improve perceptual super-resolution quality.

paragraphs: Federated learning distributes training across client devices and a coordinating server. Adaptive optimization on both sides can improve performance, but it also creates communication and memory demands that make large cross-device deployments harder. This paper develops two algorithms that retain joint adaptivity while reducing different parts of that resource burden.

FedAda² avoids transmitting preconditioners between the server and clients. These are the quantities used to adjust how optimization updates are scaled. Avoiding their transfer targets communication overhead directly. The enhanced FedAda²++ also uses memory-efficient adaptive optimizers on clients, addressing the storage demands of adaptation on individual devices. The two versions therefore target related but distinct scaling constraints.

The authors establish the same convergence rates for general non-convex objectives as more resource-intensive approaches that directly combine server and client adaptivity. Experiments on image and text datasets support both the value of joint adaptation and the proposed algorithms’ efficiency. The theoretical claim concerns convergence rates; the empirical evidence adds support for their practical effectiveness.
neurips-2025-efficient-adaptive-federate.tldr: FedAda² and FedAda²++ reduce communication and client memory costs while retaining the convergence rates of more resource-intensive jointly adaptive methods.

paragraphs: Longer reasoning does not help every visual question equally. The paper identifies a problem with applying GRPO reinforcement learning to vision-language models: training can either fail to extend useful reasoning or encourage verbose answers across tasks for only small accuracy gains. FAST-GRPO aims to make reasoning depth depend on the question instead of treating additional length as uniformly valuable.

The authors first examine how response length and the training-data distribution affect performance. Guided by those observations, they introduce two complementary measures of question difficulty. These measures inform whether fast or slow reasoning is appropriate. Training then combines adaptive rewards based on response length with a difficulty-aware KL-divergence term, adjusting how the model is encouraged to change during optimization.

Across seven reasoning benchmarks, FAST achieves reported state-of-the-art accuracy and more than 10% relative improvement over the base model. It also uses 32.7–67.3% fewer tokens than previous slow-thinking approaches. These comparisons support allocating longer reasoning selectively as a way to improve the accuracy–length tradeoff.
neurips-2025-fast-slow-thinking-grpo-for.tldr: FAST-GRPO adapts reasoning depth to question difficulty, improving reported accuracy while using fewer tokens than previous slow-thinking approaches.

paragraphs: FlexWorld addresses the challenge of turning a single image into a scene that can be explored from substantially different viewpoints. The intended exploration includes full rotations and zooming, which require content beyond what the original image shows. Limited 3D training data makes learning this capability difficult, especially when camera movement reveals large new regions.

The framework progressively builds a persistent scene representation using 3D Gaussian splatting. It synthesizes new content and integrates that content into the growing representation. To generate views under large camera changes, it uses a pretrained video model fine-tuned on training pairs with accurate estimated depth. Geometry-aware integration and optimization then refine how the generated content fits into the scene.

Experiments report better visual quality than existing state-of-the-art methods across multiple metrics and datasets for novel-view videos and flexible-view scenes. Qualitative examples demonstrate rotation and zooming capabilities. FlexWorld can also expand existing 3D scenes, extending the same progressive construction approach beyond scenes initialized from a single image.
neurips-2025-flexworld-progressively-exp.tldr: FlexWorld progressively generates and integrates 3D content into persistent scenes that support large viewpoint changes, rotation, and zooming.

paragraphs: Large pretrained time series models can forecast well without task-specific training, yet fine-tuning them does not consistently beat smaller models trained specifically for the target task. This paper asks how to adapt those broad forecasting capabilities more effectively. Its empirical starting point is that pretrained models often contain sparse activity patterns and redundant computation.

The authors interpret these patterns as evidence that different forecasting tasks use different parts of the network. They propose structured pruning before fine-tuning, removing network structure so that adaptation happens within a smaller, more relevant parameter space. Pruning acts as a form of regularization intended to preserve useful pretrained knowledge while concentrating subsequent learning on the target task.

Across seven foundation models and six benchmarks, fine-tuning pruned models significantly improves forecasting compared with fine-tuning the original models. The approach often reaches state-of-the-art results and surpasses strong specialized baselines. The finding supports task-focused model reduction as an adaptation strategy, with the reported benefits extending beyond simply having fewer parameters.
neurips-2025-less-is-more-unlocking-spec.tldr: Pruning time series foundation models before fine-tuning improves reported forecasting performance by focusing adaptation on a smaller, task-relevant network.

paragraphs: OmniCast targets probabilistic weather forecasting across both medium-range and subseasonal-to-seasonal horizons. Many forecasting models repeatedly predict the next state from earlier predictions, allowing errors to accumulate over time. OmniCast instead represents and generates a sequence of future states jointly, using a compact representation to make long sequences manageable.

A variational autoencoder compresses raw weather data into continuous latent representations. A diffusion-based transformer learns to estimate randomly hidden future tokens using the initial conditions and visible tokens. At inference, it constructs the future sequence by repeatedly filling randomly chosen subsets of hidden tokens. Joint sampling across space and time mitigates the compounding errors associated with autoregressive forecasting.

The authors report competitive medium-range performance against leading probabilistic methods while running 10–20 times faster. At subseasonal-to-seasonal horizons, they report state-of-the-art results across accuracy, physical, and probabilistic measures. They also demonstrate stable generated rollouts extending 100 years. That stability result describes long-run model behavior; it is distinct from the forecast-accuracy results at shorter horizons.
neurips-2025-omnicast-a-masked-latent-di.tldr: OmniCast jointly generates compressed future weather states, reporting fast medium-range forecasts and state-of-the-art subseasonal-to-seasonal performance.

paragraphs: Independently trained neural networks can sometimes be connected by a straight line between their parameters while keeping loss low along the path. Seeing this linear mode connectivity may first require rearranging equivalent components so that they correspond. This paper investigates that phenomenon in mixture-of-experts models, where a learned gate combines or selects among expert networks.

The authors analyze both dense and sparse gating and characterize the architectures’ symmetries through permutations involving the experts and the gating function. This matters because equivalent arrangements can look different when compared parameter by parameter. They then introduce a matching algorithm that aligns independently trained models, making it possible to search for low-loss linear connections after accounting for those symmetries.

Experiments find linear mode connectivity across dense, sparse, and shared-expert configurations, using varied model settings and datasets spanning different scales and modalities. These results extend the empirical picture of connectivity to mixture-of-experts architectures. They also provide a symmetry-based method for studying how separately trained expert systems relate within parameter space.
neurips-2025-on-linear-mode-connectivity.tldr: A symmetry-aware matching algorithm reveals low-loss linear connections between independently trained mixture-of-experts models across diverse evaluated configurations.

paragraphs: Conditional independence testing asks whether two quantities remain related after accounting for other information. Such tests support causal discovery and assessments of fairness and robustness. A known impossibility result rules out universally valid finite-sample tests with nontrivial detection power, but the authors argue that this result does not adequately explain the failures often seen in practical tests.

They investigate the Kernel-based Conditional Independence test, or KCI, to identify more concrete causes of its behavior. Their analysis also shows that the Generalized Covariance Measure, which underlies many recent tests, is nearly a special case of KCI. This connection makes the investigation relevant to a broader family of testing methods.

The paper highlights errors in estimating conditional mean embeddings as a key influence on false positives, also called Type I errors. It further identifies the conditioning kernel as an important choice: an appropriate kernel is necessary for good detection power, but also tends to inflate false positives. The analysis therefore exposes a practical tension between finding dependence and maintaining error control.
neurips-2025-on-the-hardness-of-conditio.tldr: The paper links practical conditional independence testing failures to conditional estimation errors and a kernel-choice tension between detection power and false positives.

paragraphs: The paper studies repeated decisions in which each available action is a binary vector representing a combination of choices. After choosing an action, the learner observes the full loss vector. Under the stated assumption that each action’s loss lies between −1 and 1, the question is how closely Hedge approaches the best possible regret guarantee across combinatorial action sets.

The authors establish a lower bound for every algorithm that places Hedge within a factor of the square root of log d of optimal, where d is the vector dimension. They also show this gap can be real: for m-sets with log d ≤ m ≤ square root of d, Hedge is suboptimal by exactly that factor. For online multitask learning, however, Hedge is optimal.

A further result connects Hedge to Online Mirror Descent with dilated entropy for shortest paths in directed acyclic graphs. The two produce equivalent iterates, so the mirror-descent formulation inherits Hedge’s near-optimal regret guarantees. The contribution combines a broad guarantee with precise cases showing its limits.
neurips-2025-on-the-universal-near-optim.tldr: Hedge is near-optimal across the stated combinatorial setting, with a precise logarithmic-factor gap that is attained for some action sets.

paragraphs: Estimating a person’s three-dimensional pose from indoor radar typically requires detailed 3D joint annotations during training. Those labels are costly to collect, especially with clutter, occlusion, or multiple people. RAPTR instead learns with 3D bounding boxes and 2D keypoints, which the authors describe as easier to obtain at scale.

Its transformer-based architecture uses two decoding stages and a pseudo-3D deformable attention mechanism to incorporate radar features from multiple views. The first stage estimates an initial pose. A 3D template loss uses the bounding-box labels to reduce ambiguity about depth. The second stage refines individual joints using the 2D keypoint labels together with a 3D gravity loss.

On two indoor radar datasets, RAPTR outperforms existing methods, reducing joint-position error by 34.3% on HIBER and 76.9% on MMVR. These results support the proposed combination of coarse 3D supervision, 2D joint supervision, and staged refinement. The contribution is a way to learn accurate 3D pose estimates while requiring less detailed annotation.
neurips-2025-raptr-radar-based-3d-pose-e.tldr: RAPTR learns radar-based 3D human poses from bounding boxes and 2D keypoints, reporting lower joint errors without detailed 3D keypoint labels.

paragraphs: Retrv-R1 uses step-by-step reasoning to improve multimodal retrieval. The authors identify two obstacles to transferring R1-style reinforcement learning directly to this task. Reasoning over multiple candidates consumes many tokens, making retrieval expensive. Direct reinforcement-learning training also produces instability and suboptimal results, motivating changes to both information processing and training.

The framework compresses candidate information to reduce token use and adds a mechanism for inspecting details. This is intended to retain critical information when a candidate is difficult to judge. Its training begins with an activation stage using synthetic reasoning examples tailored to retrieval. Reinforcement learning follows, with a curriculum reward designed to improve both retrieval performance and efficiency.

Across multiple benchmarks and tasks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance, high efficiency, and strong generalization. The contribution is the coordinated design: compression addresses the cost of considering candidates, detail inspection protects difficult judgments, and staged training addresses optimization problems. Together, these changes make reasoning-based retrieval more effective in the reported evaluations.
neurips-2025-retrv-r1-a-reasoning-driven.tldr: Retrv-R1 combines compressed candidate information, selective detail inspection, and staged reinforcement learning to improve multimodal retrieval.

paragraphs: RPG360 estimates depth from a single 360-degree image without additional training. It addresses the shortage of large labeled datasets for panoramic depth estimation by reusing foundation models designed for ordinary perspective images. The central challenge is making their separate predictions agree across an entire surrounding scene.

The method first converts the panorama into six faces of a cube. A perspective foundation model estimates depth and surface normals for each face. These predictions can use inconsistent depth scales, so simply combining them would not provide a coherent reconstruction. RPG360 applies graph-based optimization with parameterized depth and normal maps, including an extra scale parameter for each face, to align them while preserving 3D structure.

The authors report superior depth-estimation performance across Matterport3D, Stanford2D3D, and 360Loc, drawing on the foundation models’ zero-shot robustness. They also demonstrate benefits for feature matching and Structure from Motion. Those downstream results show that aligning the face predictions can help subsequent geometric tasks as well as panoramic depth estimation itself.
neurips-2025-rpg360-robust-360-depth-est.tldr: RPG360 combines perspective-model predictions with graph-based scale alignment to estimate coherent panoramic depth without additional training.

paragraphs: TabSTAR focuses on tables that contain free-text fields alongside other data. Language models offer a way to bring semantic knowledge into these prediction tasks, but many existing approaches use fixed text representations that do not account for the prediction target. The same textual information may therefore be represented without regard to what the model needs to infer.

TabSTAR makes its representations target-aware. It allows a pretrained text encoder to update during learning and supplies target tokens that describe the task context. This enables embeddings to adapt to the prediction objective. Its architecture also avoids dataset-specific parameters, supporting transfer learning across different tables while retaining a shared model structure.

On established classification benchmarks with text features, the authors report state-of-the-art performance for both medium-sized and large datasets. They also observe scaling laws as the number of pretraining datasets grows. These findings support combining task-sensitive language representations with cross-dataset pretraining, and suggest that expanding dataset coverage offers a path toward further improvements.
neurips-2025-tabstar-a-tabular-foundatio.tldr: TabSTAR learns target-aware text representations for tabular classification, reporting strong transfer performance and scaling with more pretraining datasets.

paragraphs: In-context reinforcement learning aims to let agents adapt from their ongoing interactions. Scaling this capability requires a large supply of training tasks, which is difficult to assemble. The paper introduces AnyMDP, a procedural generator of tabular Markov decision processes, to create tasks at scale through carefully designed randomization while maintaining relatively low structural bias.

The authors also introduce decoupled policy distillation and incorporate prior information to make large-scale meta-training more efficient. With a sufficiently large collection of AnyMDP tasks, the resulting model generalizes to tasks not considered in training through varied forms of in-context learning. The generated task supply also enables broader empirical study of how the training distribution affects adaptation.

The findings suggest that generalization may require greater task diversity and longer adaptation periods. This qualifies the benefit: broader capability need not mean reaching good behavior after only a few interactions. The authors consequently emphasize extensive, diverse task design and performance after sustained adaptation when scaling robust in-context reinforcement learning.
neurips-2025-towards-large-scale-in-cont.tldr: AnyMDP supplies scalable randomized training tasks for in-context reinforcement learning, with generalization potentially requiring more diversity and longer adaptation.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders are widely used to discover interpretable features in language models. This paper asks whether those learned features are better than features already present in the model’s own parameters. That comparison matters because assessing a feature-discovery method alone does not establish how much it improves on directly examining the original network.

The authors revisit feed-forward layers as key-value memories and evaluate their stored feature vectors using modern interpretability benchmarks. They find that feed-forward features and sparse-autoencoder features occupy a similar range of interpretability. Sparse autoencoders show observable but small advantages in some aspects, while ordinary feed-forward features perform better in certain others.

The two approaches also uncover different features, raising questions about both feature quality and faithfulness to the original model. The findings do not establish that sparse autoencoders lack value; they challenge the size and consistency of their advantage in the evaluated comparisons. Direct interpretation of feed-forward key-value parameters emerges as a strong baseline for evaluating modern interpretability methods.
neurips-2025-transformer-key-value-memor.tldr: Directly examined feed-forward features are nearly as interpretable as sparse-autoencoder features in the reported evaluations, providing a strong comparison baseline.

paragraphs: An uncertain knowledge graph attaches a confidence score to each relationship, so completing it means predicting both missing relationships and their confidence. The paper identifies an obstacle in existing embedding methods: confidence values can be extremely unevenly distributed. Ignoring that imbalance can leave the learned representations poorly suited to completing the graph.

The proposed ssCDL method transforms each confidence score into a distribution, providing a richer supervisory signal across different confidence levels. It then alternates learning from existing relationships with known scores and unseen relationships assigned generated scores. Meta-learning predicts these pseudo-labels, allowing the added examples to expand the training data and rebalance confidence coverage.

This makes confidence distribution learning and semi-supervised augmentation parts of the same iterative process. Existing labeled facts anchor learning, while pseudo-labeled relationships extend the information available to the model. Experiments on two uncertain knowledge graph datasets show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across different evaluation metrics, supporting the value of explicitly addressing confidence imbalance.
neurips-2025-uncertain-knowledge-graph-c.tldr: ssCDL improves uncertain knowledge graph completion by learning confidence distributions and using pseudo-labels to rebalance training data.

paragraphs: Direct Preference Optimization trains a language model to favor preferred responses without requiring a separate reward model. This paper examines a problematic training effect: strongly reducing the probability of an already unlikely rejected response can shift probability toward the model’s most confident output. Both preferred and rejected responses may lose confidence while unrelated tokens gain it.

VPO addresses this effect for reasoning tasks by selectively constraining negative gradients on rejected examples. It uses V-usable information to measure similarity between preference pairs and guide those constraints. The aim is to reduce undesirable probability shifts while preserving the model’s ability to distinguish preferred reasoning from rejected reasoning and better aligning training with generation.

The authors compare VPO with DPO and recent variants on mathematical reasoning using Base and Instruct models from the Llama 3.1 and Qwen 2.5 families. They report consistent, significant improvements. For Qwen2.5-7B-Base, the reported gains over DPO are 7.80% on MATH500 and 13.25% on AMC23, with ablations and further analysis examining the method’s effectiveness.
neurips-2025-vpo-reasoning-preferences-o.tldr: VPO selectively limits negative preference-training gradients to reduce harmful probability shifts and improve mathematical reasoning performance.

paragraphs: A video search query can match several separate moments, yet many temporal retrieval systems focus on finding just one. This paper addresses that mismatch with QV-M², a dataset containing 2,212 annotations covering 6,384 video segments, together with evaluation metrics designed for retrieving multiple relevant moments.

The authors also introduce FlashMMR. Its post-verification module refines proposed moment boundaries through constrained temporal adjustment, then reassesses the candidate segments with a verification module. Low-confidence proposals are removed through this filtering process. The method therefore addresses both where a retrieved segment begins and ends and whether it should remain among the final results.

Six existing methods are retrained and evaluated on QV-M² and QVHighlights in both single-moment and multi-moment settings. The results support QV-M² as a training and evaluation benchmark and FlashMMR as a strong baseline. On QV-M², FlashMMR reports improvements over the prior state of the art of 3.00% on G-mAP, 2.70% on mAP@3+tgt, and 2.56% on mR@3.
neurips-2025-when-one-moment-isn-t-enoug.tldr: QV-M² and FlashMMR advance retrieval of multiple video moments per query through a dedicated benchmark and boundary refinement with verification.
